meta.title: Montera footprint: data centers in Generation Park and Caldwell County, 21 days of posts
meta.subject: data centers, transmission and water in two places only: (1) Generation Park and northeast Houston / Harris County (Humble, Sheldon, Kingwood, Atascocita, Lake Houston, Channelview) and (2) Caldwell County, Texas (Lockhart, Luling, Martindale, the Tract and Edged campuses) — local opposition, county oversight, power and water use, tax incentives, and the developers (Montera, McCord Development, Tract, Edged). STRICT RULE: a post must name or clearly concern one of these places, Harris County or Houston officials, or these developers; anything else — statewide or national data center politics (Paxton, Talarico, Abbott, senators, Forbes), other states, other cities, or posts that only share a word like Sheldon, Crosby, Humble or Martindale (Indianapolis) — is other
meta.subtitle: Oct 1 to Oct 21, 2026. Each dot is one post with 25+ views about data centers, power or water in Generation Park, Harris County or Caldwell County, plus every post repeating an earlier one, in the lane for what it argues. Higher and bigger means more views. White means 90% or more the same words as an earlier post, with a white line back to it. Coloured lines link a post to the post it quoted or replied to. Updated twice a day.

lanes.label: Neighbors oppose (noise, land, quality of life)
lanes.description: Residents and local groups object to a data center near them — noise, lights, traffic, construction, property values, rural character or flooding — and organize to stop or delay it.

lanes.label: Water use and aquifers
lanes.description: Data centers will drain local water — aquifers, river supply, Lake Houston, groundwater districts — or need cooling water the area can't spare.

lanes.label: Power, grid and transmission lines
lanes.description: Data center load strains the grid, raises power bills or brings new transmission lines and substations (CenterPoint, Bluebonnet, LCRA, ERCOT large-load queue).

lanes.label: Counties need authority over data centers
lanes.description: Harris County, Caldwell County or cities say they need power to regulate data center siting — oversight motions, moratorium calls, permit notifications, asks to the Legislature.

lanes.label: Tax breaks and who pays
lanes.description: Abatements, tax incentives, campaign money and secrecy mean taxpayers and ratepayers subsidize developers; code-named deals hide who is behind a project.

lanes.label: Jobs, tax base and growth
lanes.description: Data center and infrastructure investment brings jobs, tax base and growth to Generation Park, northeast Houston or Caldwell County, and the region should welcome it.

lanes.label: Pushback
lanes.description: Posts doubting, mocking, fact-checking or arguing against the dominant framings.

posts.name: Texas National Security Council
posts.text:
Data centers are critical national security infrastructure, and they're also powering some of Texas's best-performing companies.

The Houston Chronicle's 2026 Chronicle 100 credits the data center buildout with helping propel several Houston firms to the top of its annual ranking:

🔹 #1 Comfort Systems USA: Revenue rose ~ 30% to $9.1 billion in 2025. Technology work, led by data centers, grew from 33% to 45% of the company's revenue, and data centers are its busiest sector for new bookings.

🔹 #3 IES Holdings: Designs and installs electrical and mechanical systems for commercial and industrial clients, including data centers.

🔹 Solaris Energy Infrastructure: An electrical infrastructure firm serving data center clients, it nearly doubled revenue to about $622 million, the second-fastest growth on the list.

When America builds the digital infrastructure that secures our future, Texas workers and Texas businesses win.
